421.title: Fret not (Psalm 37)
421.hook: don't fret because of evildoers; delight in the Lord
421.carry: the meek shall inherit the earth
421.howItsDone: Some Christians turn to Psalm 37 when struggling with envy or injustice, and its line 'the meek shall inherit the earth' is read alongside the Beatitudes in Matthew 5.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Psalm thirty-four: taste first, then see, and your line, near the brokenhearted, not the strong.

The coworker who cuts corners gets the promotion. The neighbor who never returns anything just bought a boat. The person who was cruel to you in school seems to be thriving, at least online. Say you've done things the honest way, and it hasn't paid off. It's easy to stew, to replay it in the shower, to check their profile one more time and come away worse. There's a whole psalm for that. It opens with two words that sound old-fashioned, but describe that feeling exactly.
screen: `THE CORNER-CUTTER GETS PROMOTED.` → `STEWING IN THE SHOWER.` → `TWO OLD-FASHIONED WORDS.`

segments.voice: Psalm thirty-seven, in the King James Bible: "Fret not thyself because of evildoers, neither be thou envious against the workers of iniquity." Fret, in Hebrew, is linked to a word for burning, getting heated, and verse eight sets it right beside anger and wrath. Don't heat yourself up. Notice the word thyself. Fretting is something you do to you. The person who cheated is out on their boat, and you're the one burning. The psalm says they're like grass, which withers quickly: their success is real, but it's short. Then, instead of fretting, three verbs. Trust: trust in the LORD, and do good. Delight: "Delight thyself also in the LORD; and he shall give thee the desires of thine heart." Not, you'll get whatever you want. More like, delight in God, and your desires themselves begin to change. And rest: "Rest in the LORD, and wait patiently for him: fret not thyself because of him who prospereth in his way." Fret not appears three times in the first eight verses. Then verse eleven: "But the meek shall inherit the earth; and shall delight themselves in the abundance of peace." Jesus echoes it in the Sermon on the Mount: blessed are the meek. Later, an old man speaks: "I have been young, and now am old." It's a wisdom psalm, more like advice from a grandparent than a prayer. Not everyone's experience matches every line, and the Bible has other books, like Job, that wrestle with the righteous who do suffer. But this psalm's counsel is steady: don't let someone else's wrongdoing set you on fire.

If you pray, hand the person, and the justice, to God; if not, simply set the grudge down for this minute.

422.title: As the deer (Psalm 42)
422.hook: as a deer pants for water; why are you cast down, my soul?
422.carry: why so cast down, my soul?
422.howItsDone: Some Christians turn to Psalm 42 in seasons of spiritual dryness, grief or homesickness; it is chanted in monastic daily prayer and sung in hymn versions such as "As pants the hart for cooling streams."

segments.voice: Yesterday, fret not: don't heat yourself up, and your line, the meek shall inherit the earth.

The stream bed is mostly stones now. A deer comes down the hillside to the place where the water ran in spring, and stands there, sides heaving, nose low, searching. It knows exactly what it needs. Now set a person beside that deer: someone who used to walk with the crowd on feast days, singing all the way up to the house of God, and who now lives far away, while the people around him ask, so where's your God now? Today's psalm opens with that deer. Then the writer turns around and starts talking to his own soul.
screen: `A DRY STREAM BED.` → `A THIRSTY DEER.` → `A HOMESICK SINGER.`

segments.voice: Psalm forty-two begins, in the King James Bible: "As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God." The Hebrew for those brooks means channels of water, the kind that run full in the rainy season and can shrink to nothing in a dry one, so some readers picture an animal hunting for water that's hard to find. Its heading gives it to the sons of Korah, a family of temple singers. The writer remembers leading the crowds to the house of God with shouts of joy. Now he's far off, by the Jordan and the slopes of Mount Hermon, and he says: "My tears have been my meat day and night, while they continually say unto me, Where is thy God?" Meat, in older English, simply meant food. He has been living on tears. Then the turn. He speaks to himself: "Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God." He asks his own sadness a question, then gives it a gentle instruction. Not snap out of it. Hope. The same lines come back three times, twice here and once in Psalm forty-three, one reason some readers treat the two psalms as a single poem. And between the refrains, the sadness doesn't vanish: "Deep calleth unto deep," he says, every wave going over his head. In this psalm, thirst isn't a failure of faith. It's a measure of how much someone wants God.

Answer it gently, without a lecture; if you pray, add the psalm's own words, hope thou in God, and if you don't, just keep your soul company for a while.

423.title: A very present help (Psalm 46)
423.hook: though the mountains shake into the sea, God is our refuge
423.tomorrow: create in me a clean heart
423.howItsDone: Some Christians pray Psalm 46 in times of disaster, war or fear, and it lies behind Martin Luther's hymn "A Mighty Fortress Is Our God."

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hart at the water brooks, and your line, why so cast down, my soul?

Most phones have a place for an emergency contact: one name, for the moment something goes badly wrong. People don't usually pick the most impressive person they know. They pick the one who picks up, the one who has shown up before, at two in the morning, at the side of the road. Psalm forty-six is a song about that kind of help. Months ago on this path, you met one of its lines, be still. Today, the rest of the song: the earthquake that comes before the stillness, and a river that, on any map of Jerusalem, shouldn't be there.
screen: `AN EMERGENCY CONTACT.` → `THE ONE WHO PICKS UP.` → `A RIVER THAT SHOULDN'T BE THERE.`

segments.voice: The psalm opens, in the King James Bible: "God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble." In King James English, very present means near at hand, right there. The Hebrew says it a little differently: a help in troubles, found very much. Found again and again. Help with a track record. Then the song gets loud. "Therefore will not we fear, though the earth be removed, and though the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea." Waters roar, mountains shake, nations rage. Nothing in this psalm pretends trouble isn't real. And right in the middle of the noise, verse four: "There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God." Here's the surprise. Jerusalem had no river. It had a spring, the Gihon, and water carried through tunnels, but no river running through its streets. So the psalm sings one anyway. Some readers hear it as a picture of God's presence in the middle of his people. Then verse five: God will help her, "and that right early." In the Hebrew, that's at the turning of the morning. The help arrives as the night ends. Twice the psalm repeats its chorus: "The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our refuge." And each time, one more word: Selah. Nobody knows for sure what it means. One common guess is a pause in the music. If so, the pause falls right after the line about who's with us.

If you pray, say the first verse once, slowly, God is our refuge and strength; if not, just keep breathing.

424.title: Create in me a clean heart (Psalm 51)
424.hook: David's prayer after his great wrong: a broken heart you won't despise
424.howItsDone: Psalm 51 is a prayer of repentance across the churches: Catholics, Orthodox, Anglicans and Lutherans pray it in Lent and on Ash Wednesday, and some Christians pray verse 10 before confession or at the start of the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a river in a city that had none, and your line, found very much.

The prophet Nathan walks into the palace with a story about two men in one town. One rich, with flocks and herds. One poor, with a single little ewe lamb he raised with his own children, that ate from his plate and slept in his arms. A guest arrives, and instead of taking from his own flocks, the rich man takes the poor man's lamb and serves it for dinner. King David is furious. That man deserves to die, he says. And Nathan answers with four words: "Thou art the man." David has taken Bathsheba, another man's wife, and arranged for her husband Uriah to die in battle. The heading of today's psalm places it right here, in the silence after those four words.
screen: `ONE LITTLE EWE LAMB.` → `THOU ART THE MAN.` → `THE SILENCE AFTER.`

segments.voice: Psalm fifty-one begins, in the King James Bible: "Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness." No excuses. He asks to be washed, thoroughly, and cleansed. Then verse ten: "Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me." Create. In Hebrew it's bara, the same verb as the first line of the Bible, in the beginning God created. In its usual form, the Bible uses it only with God as the one doing it. So David isn't asking for a stain remover. He's asking God to do for his heart what God did for the world: make something new where there was only chaos. Sacrifices and offerings, he says, aren't what God is after. "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise." Contrite means crushed, ground down. The thing you'd expect God to turn away from, the wreckage, is the one thing he won't refuse. Readers differ on whether the headings were part of the psalms from the start; tradition hears this one as David's own. In Latin it's called the Miserere, from its first word. Catholics, Orthodox, Anglicans and Lutherans pray it in Lent and on Ash Wednesday, and the daily prayer of some churches opens each morning with its verse fifteen: O Lord, open thou my lips.

425.title: My soul waits (Psalm 62)
425.hook: truly my soul waits upon God in silence
425.howItsDone: Many Christians practice silent prayer, sitting quietly before God without words; Quaker meetings for worship gather in shared silence, and monasteries keep set hours of quiet.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bara: not scrubbed, but made new, and your line, a clean heart.

Most waiting is noisy. Hold music, the same eight bars on a loop. Refreshing the tracking page. Checking whether the message has been read yet. Scrolling while the kettle boils, because three minutes of nothing feels unbearable. Psalm sixty-two describes a different kind of waiting. No music, no scrolling, no rehearsing what you'll say. Its heading names Jeduthun, one of the musicians of the temple, and yet the psalm's opening line, in Hebrew, is about silence.
screen: `HOLD MUSIC. REFRESH. REFRESH.` → `THREE MINUTES FEELS UNBEARABLE.` → `A QUIETER KIND OF WAITING.`

segments.voice: The King James Bible opens the psalm this way: "Truly my soul waiteth upon God: from him cometh my salvation." The Hebrew is stranger and more beautiful. Read word for word, it says something like: only toward God, my soul is silence. The word is dumiyyah, a hush, a stillness. Not a soul that's busy waiting. A soul that has gone quiet in God's direction. Then verse two: "He only is my rock and my salvation; he is my defence; I shall not be greatly moved." Greatly moved. He's honest. He expects to be shaken a little. Verse five tells his own soul, "wait thou only upon God; for my expectation is from him." And verse six repeats verse two almost exactly, except one word has gone missing. Greatly. Now it's simply, "I shall not be moved." Somewhere between the two verses, the silence has done its work. A small Hebrew word, ak, meaning only or truly, turns up six times in this short psalm, like a hand tapping the same spot. Only God. Only the rock. And the silence isn't empty. Verse eight says, "pour out your heart before him." Quiet and honesty sit side by side. Christians have built whole ways of praying on this kind of quiet: monks keeping silence through the night, Quakers gathering in waiting worship, people in every church sitting in an empty sanctuary on a weekday. The psalm doesn't promise the wait will be short. It says what to wait toward.

When thoughts come, and they will, let them pass like cars on a far road. If you pray, turn the silence toward God with no words at all; if you don't, simply let the quiet be quiet.
Dumiyyah. Hebrew for silence, stillness: the hush of a soul that has gone quiet toward God, and found a rock to stand on.

426.title: In a dry land (Psalm 63)
426.hook: my soul thirsts for you in a dry and weary land
426.howItsDone: Psalm 63 is a traditional morning psalm: Orthodox Christians read it among the six psalms at the start of Matins, and Catholics pray it at Sunday Morning Prayer in the Liturgy of the Hours.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dumiyyah, a soul gone quiet toward God, and your line, in silence, waiting.

East of Jerusalem the land falls away fast. The green gives out, and the hills turn the color of bread crust, folding down toward the Dead Sea. Shade is a rock's width. Water is a rumor. This is the wilderness of Judah. The heading of Psalm sixty-three puts David here, on the run. Which time is a fair question: he fled into that wilderness from King Saul, and years later from his own son. Either way, a man with a crown, or a claim to one, is out in the dust, and his throat is dry.
screen: `EAST OF JERUSALEM.` → `THE WILDERNESS OF JUDAH.` → `A KING ON THE RUN.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible the psalm begins: "O God, thou art my God; early will I seek thee: my soul thirsteth for thee, my flesh longeth for thee in a dry and thirsty land, where no water is." Here's what the English hides. The Hebrew word for soul is nephesh. It means life, self, a living being. But it can also mean the throat, the neck, the place where breath and water go in. So when David says my soul thirsteth, a Hebrew listener could also hear: my throat is parched. The body and the longing are one word. Read that way, thirst here isn't only a pretty metaphor. A man with a dry throat notices that what he wants most is God. Then the psalm does something unexpected for a man in a desert. It praises. "Because thy lovingkindness is better than life, my lips shall praise thee." Better than life. Better than water, then, in a place where water is life. And it moves from dawn to night. "Early will I seek thee," it says at the start, and later, "When I remember thee upon my bed, and meditate on thee in the night watches." He lies awake in the dark, in a dry land, and remembers. Because of that word early, churches pray this psalm at the start of the day. In the Orthodox morning service it is read in the half-dark, and in the Catholic Liturgy of the Hours it opens Sunday morning prayer. A desert psalm, prayed over coffee.

427.howItsDone: Many Christians pray Psalm 84 when they arrive at church or go on pilgrimage, and it is sung in hymn settings and in Brahms's German Requiem as "How lovely are thy dwellings."

segments.voice: Yesterday, nephesh, soul and also throat, and your line, thirsty for God.

Look up in an old train station, a barn, a covered market, and there's often a nest tucked on a beam where nobody can reach it. The birds didn't ask. They just moved in. Now go back to the temple in Jerusalem. Pilgrims arrive dusty from the road. And up in the stonework, little birds are building nests and raising chicks, right next to the holiest place in the land. One pilgrim noticed, and envied them.
screen: `A NEST ON A STATION BEAM.` → `BIRDS IN THE TEMPLE.` → `A PILGRIM'S ENVY.`

segments.voice: Psalm eighty-four begins, in the King James Bible: "How amiable are thy tabernacles, O LORD of hosts!" In King James English, amiable meant lovely, lovable. The Hebrew word is close to beloved. This is a love song for a place. Then verse three: "Yea, the sparrow hath found an house, and the swallow a nest for herself, where she may lay her young, even thine altars." The Hebrew word for sparrow is a general word for any small bird. The point is how small. The least important creature in the courtyard gets to live where the pilgrim can only visit. Those who travel to God's house, verse six says, pass through the valley of Baca, and make it a well. Nobody is sure what Baca means. It may be weeping, or a kind of tree that grows in dry places. Either way, the pilgrims turn a hard valley into springs as they walk through. Then the line people remember: "For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand. I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness." The heading gives this psalm to the sons of Korah. Their ancestor Korah led a rebellion against Moses, and the book of Chronicles later lists Korah's descendants among the keepers of the gates. So the people singing that they'd rather stand at the door may have been the family whose job was the door. Brahms set this psalm in his German Requiem, and congregations still sing it as a hymn.

segments.voice: Go somewhere peaceful if you can, or picture it: a bench, a window seat, a corner with the light just right; it doesn't need to be a church. Settle in like a bird on a beam, without earning the spot, and notice what makes it feel like home. If you pray, whisper the first line, How amiable are thy tabernacles, O LORD of hosts; if you don't, simply rest where you are welcome.
How lovely. Psalm eighty-four's love song for God's house, where even a sparrow builds its nest by the altar.
